metadata.title: Building Three Game Props with Claude, Blender MCP and Godot
metadata.topic: Three 3D props for HOUSEGHOST, built with Claude through the Blender MCP and checked in Godot
metadata.author: Narasimha Reddy Valam

beats.role_note: Reconstruction of the Claude composer; the opening prompt, typed, under a short spoken intro
beats.narration_text: Namaste, this is Liam, in for Bear. Today we take apart three props for HOUSEGHOST, a Godot game by Narasimha Reddy Valam, built with Claude through the Blender MCP and checked in Godot.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about HOUSEGHOST's remembered bedroom into three simple 3D props: the wind-up music box, bedside lamp and memory-only bookshelf. Work in my running Blender session through the Blender MCP, propose each build before executing it, keep the geometry and material budgets, then export to Godot and verify dimensions, orientation and origins.

beats.narration_text: This is a small part of HOUSEGHOST: three objects from a bedroom that exists in two states. A music box, a lamp, and a bookshelf. They look ordinary. In this game, they are the difference between a room that has been emptied and a room that still remembers who lived there.

shot.capture_kind: Godot engine capture — scripted camera, native 4K

show.event: label: Godot engine capture — scripted camera, native 4K

qc.full_bleed_reason: Real footage fitted to the whole frame, edge to edge, by design: the recording is the content.

beats.narration_text: Rather than treat them as isolated models, I built them as game assets. Each has a visual job, a defined size, a geometry budget, an origin, and a path from Blender into Godot. This is how that path held up.

props.title: Three props, one remembered room
props.status: My A2 art — the room they come from

beats.narration_text: HOUSEGHOST is a side-on 2D story about the ghost of a boy believed to have run away. In the empty bedroom, his belongings are gone. Turn the world over, and the remembered room comes back — warmer, lit, and full of objects with meaning.

The music box is the first relic. It calls from a place the player cannot reach directly and introduces the room’s logic. The lamp establishes the warmth of memory. The bookshelf exists as solid geometry only in the remembered state, so it matters to navigation, not just decoration.

props.title: Each prop has a job
props.imageLabel: the three final props, side by side

beats.narration_text: The main game is 2D, but these props also live in a separate 3D Godot showcase. That lets me inspect their actual scale, orientation and materials without pretending they are already integrated into the side-scroller.

I started by fixing a scale instead of guessing by eye. The player's collision capsule is 250 pixels high, so I used 250 pixels per metre as the working conversion. That makes the bookshelf one metre tall — the height of the capsule that it blocks.

props.title: One metre is 250 pixels
tree: Floor to ceiling, interior — 800 px — 3.20 m

beats.narration_text: The illustration isn't perfectly consistent with that measurement. A later check showed the boy's standing drawing was 341 pixels, or 1.36 metres, rather than the 1.28 metres first quoted in the brief. The brief now records that correction; the collider-based scale did not change.

props.title: The art disagrees with itself
tree: Brief, as written — sprite 320 px — 1.28 m

notes.label: Why
notes.value: anchored on the collider, not the drawing

beats.narration_text: Before any model was built, I committed a brief with dimensions, materials, origins and triangle limits for all three objects. I also wrote down seven ways the process might fail: wrong orientation, wrong scale, misplaced origin, excess geometry, colour changes, a connected-but-unusable MCP, and an object that passes every numeric check but still looks wrong. Those predictions became the inspection plan.

props.title: Seven predictions, committed first
props.source: CHANGE-BRIEF.md — committed 722658f, 2026-10-14 17:48, before any build (Repository file)
tree: 7 — right by every number, still wrong

beats.narration_text: First, I learned the window I was about to direct: the viewport for looking, the Outliner for objects, Properties for materials and scene settings, the sidebar for exact transforms, the toolbar for interaction, and the mode selector for object-level versus mesh-level editing.

Then I checked the connection itself. A client saying ‘connected’ is not proof it can control Blender. I asked Claude to call `get_scene_info` before building anything. It returned the live default scene — cube, camera and light. That confirmed the MCP could read the running session.

props.title: Connected is not controlling
props.source: get_scene_info — first call, before any build (Command output)
tree: Scene 'Scene' | 1 camera, 1 light, 1 mesh | active Cube | mode OBJECT

notes.label: Proves
notes.value: the MCP reads my live session

beats.narration_text: The add-on was bound to localhost on port 9876, verified with `lsof`. I left remote model-download and generation services disabled. The geometry in this film was built locally from Blender shapes, not imported from an asset library.

props.title: Local only, generators off
props.imageLabel: MCP for Blender: connected on port 9876; libraries and generators off

beats.narration_text: Here is the collaboration in practice. I told Claude to go ahead with the bookshelf, and its first reply laid the build out in numbers: six boards, with dimensions, materials, bevels and a triangle estimate — 296 triangles against a 360-triangle target. For each redesign that followed, nothing ran until I had approved the plan.

Claude then created the pieces through `execute_blender_code`, one object at a time. After each operation it queried the scene again to read the resulting position, dimensions, rotation and scale. The geometry was built at its intended size, with identity object transforms.

props.title: What it built
props.status: Captured in my Blender session via the MCP
props.imageLabel: left: what that prompt built · right: the approved final

beats.narration_text: Every executed call body is kept in `tools/blender`, alongside scripts that rebuild each source file from an empty scene. That means the final `.blend` files are not the only record of how the objects were made.

beats.narration_text: This is the final music box. The first version was within the limits: five basic shapes, 252 triangles, and a lid opened eighteen degrees. But it was too generic. It met the numbers without delivering the presence I wanted.

shot.capture_kind: Capture of my Blender session — camera driven via the MCP

show.event: label: Capture of my Blender session — camera driven via the MCP

qc.full_bleed_reason: Real footage fitted to the whole frame, edge to edge, by design: the recording is the content.

beats.narration_text: I used a generated image as a design reference, not as a mesh. The assignment allows six basic shapes, and my budget was 320 triangles, so we kept only what fits: a hollow body with a darker cavity, a raised plinth, the opened lid, a clasp, and a key with a simple oval bow in line with its shaft. The hinges, the tray-shaped lid and the holes in the key were left out to stay within those limits.

props.title: A reference, not a mesh
props.imageLabel: left: the reference · right: my final build, within six shapes

cards.label: Left out
cards.text: hinges, tray lid, holes in the key

beats.narration_text: The body uses an inset and extrusion to create twelve-millimetre walls and a ten-centimetre cavity. A small gap at the lid's hinge was closed, and the new silhouette checked. The finished model uses 312 triangles against a 320-triangle budget. Small bevels catch the light; face-weighted normals help the flat faces shade cleanly.

props.title: Twelve-millimetre walls
props.status: Captured in my Blender session via the MCP

beats.narration_text: This is the final lamp. The first one followed the original painting: a traditional base and cone shade. I replaced it with a quieter modern silhouette — ceramic base, brass collar and broad drum shade. I revised its triangle budget from 340 to 420 before building, documenting why the curved base needed more geometry.

show.event: label: Capture of my Blender session — camera driven via the MCP

qc.full_bleed_reason: Real footage fitted to the whole frame, edge to edge, by design: the recording is the content.

beats.narration_text: The modern reference set its shape; within six shapes, its open top became a closed shade with a brass finial. The showcase scene allows one light, so an internal lamp light was ruled out, and the lamp’s glow lives in its shade material instead.

props.title: One scene light
props.imageLabel: left: the reference · right: my final lamp

cards.label: Kept
cards.text: pill base, drum shade, collar, foot

cards.label: Scene
cards.text: one light; glow in the shade

beats.narration_text: The first Godot import exposed a problem the Blender numbers could not: emission at 1.0 pushed the cream shade to clipped white. We lowered the source emission to 0.4, rebuilt, re-exported and re-imported. The cream returned, and the source, export and rendered result agreed.

The bookshelf was deliberately simple: six boards, warm wood, a modern profile with rounded top corners. Its first version passed the dimensional and transform checks. It still missed the feature that made the design recognizable: the upper corners were square.

props.title: Six boards, rounded corners
props.imageLabel: left: the reference · right: my final bookshelf

beats.narration_text: The issue was the order of bevel operations. An earlier edge bevel caused Blender's overlap clamp to reduce the intended three-centimetre rounding to about three millimetres. Reordering the operations restored the shape.

props.title: Order of operations
props.status: Captured in my Blender session via the MCP — final version
props.excerpt: bevel(top_corners, offset=0.03, segments=4) — before the front-edge bevel

beats.narration_text: Claude added an assertion for the corrected geometry. That check initially contained its own local-versus-world coordinate mistake, which was corrected too. A passing test is useful only when the test is measuring what I think it measures.

props.title: A test that measures what it means
tree: rounded corners: 2 | front edges: 2 | front face top z = 0.9700 (expect 0.9700)
first run: AssertionError — local height compared with world height

notes.label: Asserts
notes.value: front face stops 3 cm below the top

beats.narration_text: I also changed the bookshelf myself in Blender's window. I duplicated a shelf and moved the new one toward the base, so the open space felt more deliberately divided.

props.title: Before my edit
props.status: Captured in my Blender session via the MCP
props.imageLabel: two shelves and a back panel — 248 triangles

beats.narration_text: That small edit taught me how precise the interface needs to be. My first duplication included the selected parent and created a second root. A free gizmo drag shifted the shelf sideways as well as vertically, and Blender made a duplicate material. Inspecting the Outliner and transforms showed each of those, and taught me that a free drag moves every axis at once, while the axis arrow keeps it to one.

props.title: What the edit taught me
props.imageLabel: duplicate with its parent · drift on every axis · a seventh board

beats.narration_text: The extra shelf took the model over six boards. I chose to remove the back panel rather than lose the new shelf, preserving the open-backed direction of the original brief. Claude then re-centred the shelves at my heights, cleaned up the duplicate objects and material, and brought the reproducible build script into agreement with the edited scene. The final bookshelf uses six boards and 280 triangles.

props.title: After my edit
props.status: Captured in my Blender session via the MCP — same camera

beats.narration_text: A Blender model is not finished when it looks good in Blender. Each asset was exported as a binary `.glb` with plus-Y up. A separate reader inspected the exported files for colours, transforms and orientation before Godot loaded them.

props.title: Read the exported file itself
tree: asset: Khronos glTF Blender I/O v5.2.40 | up axis: glTF is always +Y up
node BS_Shelf_Bottom translation [0, 0.12, 0.0015] | no rotation, no scale
size x 0.64 | y (up) 1.0 | z 0.3 | lowest point y = 0.0

beats.narration_text: Then a Godot headless script read each imported asset's bounding box, node scales, vertical axis and lowest point.

props.title: Compose the transforms yourself

notes.label: Why
notes.value: global_transform is identity outside the tree

notes.label: Checks
notes.value: size · scale · up axis · lowest point

beats.narration_text: Here are the results beside the original targets. All three fall within two millimetres of the specified dimensions, stand along Y, have unit scales and measure down to zero.

props.title: Headless check — not a visual check
tree: every node scale 1, 1, 1 · height along Y · lowest point 0.0000

beats.narration_text: The first version of that script failed every correct asset because it asked for global transforms before the objects were in the scene tree. Claude corrected it to compose transforms explicitly, and it was tested against a deliberately wrong height, which it rejects. The output is a measurement, not a substitute for looking at the scene.

props.title: A check must be able to fail
props.source: check_assets.gd against a deliberately wrong height (Command output)
tree: FAIL: Bookshelf: size differs from the brief by more than 2 mm
FAIL: Bookshelf: height does not lie along Y (lying on its side?)
What it cannot prove: how an asset looks · contact with a floor

beats.narration_text: The scene uses Godot's Compatibility renderer, consistent with the main 2D project. The sky lighting was adjusted when the brass appeared almost black. That was a presentation issue the geometry checks would never catch.

props.title: Lit for the materials
props.imageLabel: the scene open in my Godot editor

beats.narration_text: Finally, I inspected each object from behind, from below and at an angle. The bookshelf reads correctly, and the lamp keeps its intended silhouette and colour. The music box has no missing faces, but from behind its small key disappears visually, so it can read as an ordinary box. That remains a real design limitation.

props.title: Behind, below, at an angle
props.imageLabel: my orbit check: rear · bottom · angled, cropped to the 3D view

beats.narration_text: The result is three game-scale props, built in a live Blender workflow, exported as `.glb`, and visible together in Godot. Their final triangle counts are 312 for the music box, 406 for the lamp, and 280 for the bookshelf — each within its own budget and the course limit of 500.

artifactLines: Music box — 312 triangles, budget 320.
Lamp — 406 triangles, budget 420.
Bookshelf — 280 triangles, budget 360. Course limit: 500 each.
Built live in Blender, exported as .glb, shown in Godot.

beats.narration_text: I verified the sizes, orientations, origins, object scales and colours across Blender, the exported files and Godot. I also inspected the actual renders and the assets from multiple angles. Those checks agree on the measurable properties; they cannot certify that an object reads correctly under every lighting condition.

artifactLines: Size, orientation, origin, scale and colour.

beats.narration_text: The revisions were substantive. I redesigned a too-simple music box, replaced the lamp silhouette, fixed a shade that clipped to white, recovered the bookshelf's rounded corners, and Claude cleaned up my manual shelf edit. Claude also made errors in geometry selection, normals logic, exporter validation and the Godot check itself. I kept the specific failures and corrections in the test report rather than presenting the final pass as if it happened on the first try.

artifactLines: A music box rebuilt with real presence.
A lamp redesigned; its shade un-clipped.
The bookshelf's rounded corners recovered.
Claude's errors kept in the test report.

qc.sparse_reason: The course's verdict card: short numbered lines on a white card, which the gate's ink detector cannot see against the cream stage, so it measures only the text. Not underfilled.

beats.narration_text: My role was to define the game context and brief, choose and reject designs, approve builds, edit geometry in Blender, inspect the visual results and decide which tradeoffs to keep. Claude wrote and executed the modeling and checking code under that direction, with its outputs preserved for review.

artifactLines: Me: the brief, the designs, approvals, the hand edit,
the visual judgement and the trade-offs.
Claude: the modelling and checking code,
run under that direction, outputs preserved.

beats.narration_text: What remains uncertain is how the props will read in the finished game's actual room lighting, whether the music box is identifiable from behind, and how another viewer would interpret the scene. My next step is to improve the music box's rear silhouette without exceeding six shapes or 320 triangles.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Please use Walker to improve my music box's silhouette from behind, within the same six shapes and 320 triangles. Predict how it will read before you build it, then compare real Godot editor views from behind and from the left. It aims at the one thing this film found the checks could not: a box that passes every number but does not read from behind. Take this prompt to your own model, and test the result twice — with measurements, and with your own eyes. Liam, in for Bear.
